items.title: COP collapse
items.description: THE collapse of climate negotiations at COP31 in Antalya recently is a stark reminder of a world disinclined to cooperate for the common good. The first climate conference to end without a deal since the 2009 Copenhagen Summit, COP31 succumbed to entrenched divisions among the delegates. The main sticking point was the phasing out of fossil fuels , which was not mentioned in the draft agreement because of pressure from the petro-states including Saudi Arabia and Russia. This omission was rejected by the EU, Britain, and some small, climate-vulnerable states, which rightly hold fossil fuels responsible for global warming. Another stumbling block was the lack of commitment to providing climate finance. Ironically, many of the countries that opposed the deal for not including the transition away from fossil fuels, refused to move forward on earlier pledges to provide and mobilise funding for poor climate-vulnerable countries. It has been noted, in fact, that many of the latter prefer funds over curbs on fossil fuels at this stage, given their need to rehabilitate lives already impacted by climate change and build infrastructure strong enough to withstand future shocks. This may have been one reason why some vulnerable countries curtailed their objections to the draft deal. Day by day, the climate question is assuming greater urgency. Indeed, nature has been unrelenting against the backdrop of COP31. While Pakistan was largely spared the onrush of swelling rivers this year, Nepal witnessed a tragedy when a massive glacier collapse led to the flooding of vast tracts of land, killing hundreds. Heatwaves in Europe reportedly killed over 50,000 people last summer, while wildfires in Spain and France forced thousands of families from their homes. “Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5°C raises the risk of irreversible changes […] along with devastating human impacts,” warns the UN’s main environmental agency in its latest Emissions Gap report. The need for cooperation and consensus on tackling climate change has never been greater. Luckily, the failure of COP31 does not spell the end of climate diplomacy. International regimes built over years to combat a danger that knows no borders are too far advanced to come undone because an agreement was not reached in Antalya. But time is running out. Given national interests and the nature of geopolitics, absolute consensus may be hard to forge. However, smaller regional initiatives, where countries — especially of the developing world — share green technology and other climate-friendly solutions can be pursued. These countries — which pollute the least but bear the brunt of global warming — have every right to ask for funds from the world’s chief polluters. The question is whether they have the will to safeguard their future through collective action. Published in Dawn, November 24th, 2026

items.title: Plateau proposes recruitment of 5,000 to 7,000 personnel for state police
items.description: By Golok Nanmwa, Jos The Plateau State Government has proposed the recruitment of between 5,000 and 7,000 personnel for the proposed Plateau State Police Service as part of efforts to strengthen security and tackle rising insecurity across the state. The proposal was disclosed by the chairman of the 14-member Plateau State Advisory Committee on State Police, retired Deputy Inspector-General of Police Habila Joshak, during the presentation of the committee’s interim report to the state government on Tuesday in Jos. “We propose an implementation roadmap for recruiting between 5,000 and 7,000 personnel, with pilot deployments in flashpoint areas before statewide coverage,” Joshak said. He said, “The proposed recruitment and phased deployment are part of measures to ensure that the service is properly structured and positioned to respond to security challenges across the state.” Joshak said, “Consultations with stakeholders in the Northern and Central zones recorded overwhelming support for the establishment of state police, provided adequate safeguards are put in place against political intimidation, ethnic and religious bias, and human rights abuses.” He said the committee recommended seven major pillars, including a legal framework, zonal and divisional command structures, 24-hour operations, an independent Police Service Commission with a civilian majority, inter-agency collaboration and phased implementation. “The committee’s work is not yet complete, and we stand ready to continue it, refining our proposals and the draft legislative instruments as the constitutional alteration process unfolds,” he said. Earlier, the Secretary of the committee, Julie Sanda, said, “The committee has spent seven months undertaking research, reviewing security structures and consulting stakeholders across the three senatorial districts and the 17 local government areas of the state.” She said, “We established seven subcommittees to examine different aspects of the proposed state police service and engaged the Plateau State House of Assembly, the Association of Local Governments of Nigeria, traditional and religious leaders, women and youth groups, civil society organisations, professional associations and transport unions.” Sanda said, “Stakeholders expressed support for the establishment of state police but emphasised the need for adequate safeguards against political manipulation, ethnic bias and human rights abuses.” She added that, “The committee is proposing a proactive, community-orientated and accountable police service that will be responsive to the security needs of the people.” According to her, “An online consultation portal was also launched to enable members of the public to contribute to the process, while the interim report and draft legislative proposals reflect the concerns and aspirations expressed during the consultations.” The Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Philemon Dafi, SAN, described the proposed state police service as a practical necessity in view of the security realities confronting Plateau State. Dafi said, “Plateau State has become the first state in the country to make structured progress towards operationalising state police.” He disclosed that the committee had prepared the draft Plateau State Police Service Establishment Law, 2026, and the Plateau State Police Service Regulation, 2026, to provide the legal foundation for the proposed service. He said, “The assignment was to develop a comprehensive framework that would address the constitutional and legal requirements, security challenges, feasibility, recruitment, training, discipline and inter-agency coordination.” Dafi said consultations were still ongoing across the 17 local government areas through the official online portal and regional stakeholder validation workshops. He, however, noted that constitutional amendments by the National Assembly and the development of a national policing framework were necessary before further implementation could take place. Representing Governor Caleb Mutfwang, the Deputy Governor, Ngo Josephine Piyo, said, “The security challenges confronting our state require thoughtful, innovative and sustainable solutions.” She said, “The proposed state police service, if established within the provisions of the Constitution, will provide an additional layer of security and strengthen efforts to protect lives and property.” Piyo added that “the proposed state police service must not merely be another institution. It must be one that commands public trust, respects human rights and upholds the highest standards of professionalism and accountability.” She said the state government would study the committee’s interim report and continue consultations before taking further steps. Piyo assured that “the safety and well-being of our people remain a priority of the Mutfwang administration.” ”” The 14-member committee was inaugurated by Governor Mutfwang on March 10, 2026, with a mandate to develop the legal, operational, financial and oversight frameworks for the proposed Plateau State Police Service in anticipation of the amendment of Sections 214 to 216 of the 1999 Constitution. The post Plateau proposes recruitment of 5,000 to 7,000 personnel for state police appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Orpaillage clandestin : de Siguiri à Kissidougou et Faranah, le grand retour des ressortissants
items.description: Depuis l’arrêt des activités d’orpaillage clandestin dans les zones aurifères de Siguiri, Mandiana et Kouroussa, un vaste mouvement de retour s’observe en direction de Faranah et de Kissidougou. Hommes, femmes et enfants regagnent progressivement leurs localités d’origine, emportant avec eux leurs bagages et, pour certains, leurs dernières économies. Entre retrouvailles familiales, pertes financières, inquiétudes économiques et espoir d’un nouveau départ, cette vague de retours soulève d’importants enjeux sociaux et économiques. L’effervescence est particulièrement perceptible dès les premières heures de la journée dans les gares routières de Faranah et de Kissidougou. Les arrivées se succèdent à un rythme inhabituel. En provenance des zones aurifères de Siguiri, Mandiana et Kouroussa, des dizaines de véhicules déversent quotidiennement leurs passagers. Camions-bennes, véhicules bâchés, voitures personnelles et minibus participent à ce mouvement qui prend de plus en plus d’ampleur. Selon les constats effectués sur place, plus d’une centaine de véhicules peuvent être enregistrés chaque jour. Le spectacle est saisissant. À bord de ces véhicules, hommes, femmes et enfants voyagent au milieu de matelas, de lits, de chaises, de sacs et d’autres effets personnels. Dans certains camions-bennes et véhicules bâchés, passagers et bagages s’entassent dans des conditions particulièrement difficiles, faute d’espace suffisant. Derrière ces scènes de débarquement se dessine une réalité humaine et sociale : celle de milliers de ressortissants contraints de quitter les zones minières à la suite de l’arrêt des activités d’exploitation aurifère clandestine. Pour beaucoup, Faranah et Kissidougou ne sont que des étapes sur un long parcours vers leurs localités d’origine. Les destinations sont multiples : Guéckédou, Macenta, N’Zérékoré, Banian, Tiro, Douako, Sandénia ou encore Kobikoro. Certains poursuivent même leur voyage jusqu’en Sierra Leone. Des familles entre soulagement et inquiétude Dans les concessions familiales, ces arrivées ne passent pas inaperçues. Pour certains parents, c’est l’occasion de retrouver des enfants qu’ils n’avaient pas revus depuis plusieurs mois, voire plusieurs années. Pour d’autres, ces retours nourrissent l’espoir de voir bientôt leurs propres enfants quitter les zones minières. Les téléphones sonnent davantage et les appels se multiplient entre parents et enfants encore présents à Siguiri. Certains encouragent leurs proches à rentrer avant qu’il ne soit trop tard. Au sein d’une partie de la population, ce mouvement est accueilli favorablement. Beaucoup estiment que le départ massif des jeunes vers les sites aurifères avait progressivement vidé les villages de leur main-d’œuvre agricole. Rencontré sur place, Fara Kamano considère l’arrêt de l’orpaillage clandestin comme une occasion de ramener la jeunesse vers les activités champêtres. « L’interdiction de l’exploitation clandestine de l’or, moi, je dirais que c’est bon. Nos villages d’ici, remarquez par vous-mêmes, il n’y avait presque plus de jeunes pour les travaux champêtres. Ils étaient tous à Siguiri dans les mines. C’est ce qui faisait qu’on achetait davantage de riz importé. Les gens disent que ça ne travaille plus au pays kissi, certains nous traitent même de maudits. Ils ne savent pas ce qui se passe réellement ici », témoigne-t-il. Avec amertume, il évoque les difficultés rencontrées dans certaines localités pour mobiliser des jeunes autour des travaux agricoles. « Dans certains villages de Kissidougou et même de Guéckédou, pour tuer un coq, on avait du mal à trouver un jeune garçon, à part les tout-petits. Ils n’ont qu’à revenir. Nous, c’est la daba que nous connaissons ici. C’est avec ça que nous avons vécu et soutenu nos familles jusqu’à présent », poursuit-il. Mais derrière cette satisfaction se cache également une réalité familiale douloureuse. Le même interlocuteur affirme que plusieurs de ses enfants étaient partis dans les zones minières. Selon les informations que lui ont rapportées ses autres enfants, l’un d’eux serait actuellement en détention. « Moi-même, j’avais mes enfants là-bas. L’un est même en prison, selon ses frères. Vous pensez que c’est avec mon accord qu’ils sont partis ? Mais quand un enfant se sent grand, il fuit. Tu ne peux pas aller le chercher. Ce que je demande aux autorités, c’est de libérer ceux qui sont en prison et de faire en sorte qu’ils puissent tous rentrer chez eux », plaide-t-il. Le retour des jeunes, un nouveau défi pour les communautés Si les retrouvailles suscitent de la joie, l’arrivée massive de ces ressortissants soulève une autre préoccupation : comment assurer leur réinsertion une fois de retour dans leurs localités d’origine ? À Faranah, certains habitants redoutent les difficultés d’adaptation de ces anciens travailleurs, habitués aux revenus générés par les activités minières. En l’absence de perspectives économiques immédiates, leur retour pourrait accentuer la précarité au sein de nombreuses familles. Ibrahima Keita, un habitant rencontré dans la ville, exprime ouvertement ses inquiétudes. « Les voitures ne font que rentrer et elles sont bien chargées. Des hommes, des femmes, des enfants et leurs bagages : matelas, lits, chaises et autres effets. Aujourd’hui, notre peur à Faranah, c’est de savoir comment faire la réinsertion de ceux qui sont en train de revenir. Ils sont habitués à l’argent des mines. S’ils ne trouvent pas de travail, beaucoup risquent de se retrouver dans des difficultés. Nous demandons à tout le monde de veiller sur ses enfants et de bien garder ses effets », explique-t-il. À ces préoccupations s’ajoutent les pertes financières enregistrées par certains travailleurs. Plusieurs d'entre eux affirment avoir abandonné une partie de leurs économies dans les zones minières, notamment des cotisations versées dans des systèmes de tontines. « Certains disent qu’ils ont tout perdu. Ils expliquent qu’ils étaient dans des tontines et qu’avec cette situation, tout le monde est parti. D’autres n’ont même pas pu récupérer leur argent. Ce que je déplore, c’est que si les gens n’ont pas été avertis, ce n’est pas normal. Mais s’ils avaient été avertis, ils n’ont qu’à assumer », déplore-t-il. L’arrêt des activités aurifères ne touche pas uniquement les personnes directement impliquées dans l’exploitation de l’or. Ses répercussions se font également sentir dans les circuits commerciaux et au sein des familles qui dépendaient, de près ou de loin, de l’économie minière. À Kissidougou, Fatoumata Diallo, commerçante spécialisée dans la vente de riz, témoigne de la baisse brutale de ses activités. Les ouvriers des mines constituaient une part importante de sa clientèle et lui permettaient d’écouler quotidiennement d’importantes quantités de marchandises. « Je plains les autorités parce que nos business ont été arrêtés brusquement. Moi, je faisais le commerce du riz et ce sont les ouvriers qui étaient nos clients. Je vendais beaucoup, presque un sac chaque jour. Aujourd’hui, on se demande ce que nous allons devenir et si un jour les activités vont reprendre », raconte-t-elle. Dans son propre foyer, les conséquences de cette situation sont également perceptibles. Sa jeune sœur, enceinte, vivait avec un ressortissant burkinabè qui a finalement regagné son pays à la suite de ces événements. « J’ai une jeune sœur qui est même enceinte. Le Burkinabè est rentré. Qu’est-ce que nous allons faire maintenant ? Ce n’est pas de sa faute non plus. Le jour où il partait, il a beaucoup pleuré. Heureusement, il a laissé de l’argent et quelques objets à ma sœur. Nous sommes tous revenus ici. Mais on se demande si un jour les activités vont reprendre », confie-t-elle. Ce témoignage met en lumière une autre dimension du phénomène : des couples séparés, des familles fragilisées et des projets de vie brutalement interrompus par l’arrêt des activités minières. Entre agriculture et tensions familiales, des avis partagés Dans les rues et les concessions de Kissidougou, les réactions face à cette vague de retours sont loin d’être unanimes. Si certains y voient une occasion de relancer l’agriculture et de réunir les familles, d’autres portent un regard plus critique sur les départs massifs vers les zones aurifères. Pour un autre habitant de la ville, cette situation devrait servir de leçon à ceux qui avaient abandonné les activités agricoles et leurs responsabilités familiales pour rejoindre les sites miniers. « C’est bien fait pour nos parents. Ils ont laissé les terres à cultiver ici pour aller se promener dans les mines. Certains hommes et certaines femmes ont abandonné leurs familles et leurs enfants pour aller à Siguiri. Ici, beaucoup de femmes ne respectaient plus leurs maris parce que, dès qu’il y avait un problème, elles pliaient bagage pour aller à Siguiri », affirme-t-il. Il attire également l’attention sur la forte présence des enfants parmi les personnes qui regagnent actuellement la Guinée forestière. « Toutes les femmes qui reviennent, certaines sont venues avec trois ou quatre enfants. Les papas, eux, sont presque tous partis. Madame, regardez vous-mêmes à la gare le nombre d’enfants qui sont revenus », ajoute-t-il. Pour cet interlocuteur, le retour des ressortissants doit être l’occasion de renouer avec les activités agricoles, de valoriser les terres cultivables et de restaurer les équilibres familiaux fragilisés par l’exode vers les zones minières. Après les mines, l’épreuve de la reconstruction À Faranah comme à Kissidougou, les véhicules continuent d’arriver. Chaque débarquement raconte une histoire particulière : des familles qui se retrouvent, des biens transportés dans des conditions difficiles, des économies parfois abandonnées et des lendemains incertains. Dans les concessions, l’attente se poursuit pour les parents dont les enfants sont encore dans les zones aurifères. Les appels téléphoniques se multiplient et les espoirs de retrouvailles grandissent au rythme des arrivées. Mais au-delà de l’émotion et de la satisfaction de retrouver les siens, une question essentielle demeure : quelles perspectives économiques pour ces nombreux ressortissants qui regagnent leurs localités sans aucune garantie d’emploi ? La réinsertion professionnelle, la relance des activités agricoles, l'accompagnement des familles et la protection des personnes les plus vulnérables constituent désormais des enjeux majeurs pour les communautés d'accueil et les autorités concernées. Car l'arrêt de l'orpaillage clandestin ne signifie pas seulement la fin d'une activité pour des milliers de travailleurs. Il marque aussi le début d'une nouvelle épreuve : celle de reconstruire une vie loin des sites miniers. De Siguiri, Mandiana et Kouroussa vers Faranah et Kissidougou, le grand retour est bel et bien engagé. Reste désormais à transformer cette vague de retours en une véritable opportunité de reconstruction économique, sociale et familiale.

items.title: The Best Place to Buy Face Wash and Frozen Orange Chicken
items.description: Earlier this year, when Trader Joe’s released a list of the 11 products its customers loved the most, a bright-pink tub of Brazil Nut Body Butter was featured among the potato chips and ice-cream sandwiches. The $6 moisturizing lotion was much cheaper than similar items on the market, the announcement noted. But its fans already knew that it was a close match for the popular $48 Sol de Janeiro Brazilian Bum Bum Cream and that the TJ’s lotion had both a similar ingredient list and a similar scent of pistachio, salted caramel, and vanilla (if a less embarrassing name). That body butter is just one of the many TJ’s skin-care products that bear a striking resemblance to expensive cult favorites. The $10 vitamin C might stand in for SkinCeuticals’ $185 version. The TJ’s facial sunscreen rubs in as cleanly as a $38 Supergoop formulation. Just as Trader Joe’s snack fanatics have long tried to prove that the grocer uses the same manufacturers as name-brand favorites, people on beauty Subreddits are judging how closely TJ’s beauty offerings mimic the brands they’d find at Sephora. Like most grocery stores, Trader Joe’s has sold a limited selection of personal-care items for years. But more recently it has pushed further and further beyond the realm of lotion and tissues to offer skin-care products usually priced at a premium. Dermatologists and beauty publications now take TJ’s seriously as a beauty supplier; influencers (only semi-)joke that it’s “the next Sephora.” Buying Milky Hydrating Bi-Phase Face Mist from a store known for its frozen orange chicken might sound a little weird. But Trader Joe’s was built on what the beauty world calls “dupes,” which, in recent years, beauty consumers have become more primed to accept. Since opening its first store in the 1960s, the grocer has perfected this strategy for food. Its aisles are full of products that might remind you of other ones—instead of Oreos, they have Joe-Joe’s; instead of Swedish Fish, they have Scandinavian Swimmers. By outsourcing manufacturing to third parties, then selling the products under its private label, Trader Joe’s can undercut the competition on price. The company declined to provide details on its beauty-manufacturing process, but many beauty companies similarly use contract manufacturers, Alexis Wolfer, a McKinsey partner who’s the head of its North American beauty practice, told me. And over the past five years, those manufacturers have started “giving new or mass brands access to a lot of very similar advanced formulations that once belonged exclusively to the big houses,” she said. They’ve effectively democratized the supply chain to keep up with consumer demand for cheap, high-quality products—in effect matching what Trader Joe’s has been able to do for years with its food offerings. In some cases, Trader Joe’s and other skin-care-dupe companies can offer lower prices largely because another company already invested funds into developing the formula, Kelly Dobos, a cosmetic chemist at the University of Cincinnati, told me. About a year after the patent expired on SkinCeuticals’ original C E Ferulic serum—which pioneered a way to stabilize vitamin C, a notoriously fickle cosmetic ingredient—Trader Joe’s launched a similar formulation for $10. A leader of TJ’s beauty and health division said on the company’s podcast that she got the idea to carry a gel moisturizer after trying an expensive name-brand one. She asked one of the company’s suppliers to formulate something similar for cheaper and eventually got the $9 Ultra Hydrating Gel Moisturizer, which people now compare to a $65 formulation from Clinique. People now are also generally more willing to believe that a $10 serum can be as good as a $185 one. Dupes have been around for decades, but they took off on social media around 2022 ; by 2023, the obsession had trickled down to the mainstream enough that nearly one in three U.S. adults said they’d intentionally bought a dupe of a premium product. Just because two products have the same ingredient list doesn’t mean they’ll be equally effective, but over the years, the percentage of consumers who told McKinsey they believe that mass-beauty products can be as good as prestige ones has risen and is now at 63 percent. Whereas shoppers used to pick one price level and stick to it—your grandmother who only got her skin care at the department store, for instance—now people are more open to a good product wherever they find it. “There really isn’t the premium-beauty shopper and the mass-beauty shopper anymore,” Wolfer said. One person’s toiletry bag might contain a TJ’s cleanser they love and a $40 face mask from Sephora. Some of this price-point agnosticism is because of inflation. But people are also generally more aware of skin-care ingredients than they used to be and might be more willing to bet that Trader Joe’s $10 vitamin C serum could do its job about as well as the $185 SkinCeuticals version. That anyone who is not a dermatologist has an opinion about vitamin C serum is a sign of the “TikTok-ification of beauty,” as Wolfer put it. Beauty influencers and TikTok dermatologists, for instance, have exposed more people to Sephora “shopping haul” videos and the virtues of hyaluronic acid. And a company that wants to feed the beauty-TikTok beast can’t make just one good lotion—it has to make new ones frequently, and maybe throw in a weird ingredient people can try, like Irish sea moss, for good measure. Trader Joe’s is already set up to meet such a constant demand for new stuff (and it does carry a night cream that contains Irish-sea-moss extract). The store’s product lineup changes every week, as new products are introduced, Nakia Rohde, a Trader Joe’s spokesperson, told me. That means that the beauty aisle changes a lot as well, gaining at least one new product in October and two so far this month. Each new item doesn’t have to be terribly different from its predecessors—I doubt the company had to go back to the drawing board for its Cinnamon Roll Flavored Lip Mask after launching a vanilla-flavored one. But when one item has run its course on social media and in people’s medicine cabinets, Trader Joe’s is ready to push another on shoppers (most recently, the Espresso & Cream Flavored Lip Mask). “That also means they’ll just cut a product” out of the blue, Mark Gardiner, the author of Build a Brand Like Trader Joe’s , told me—which can motivate shoppers to pick up an extra bottle of that Supergoop-esque sunscreen, in case it’s not there the next time they visit. How someone feels about their lip mask or sunscreen—or any product, really—may depend on how much they enjoyed the shopping experience. You could purchase essentially the same body butter at CVS or Sephora or Bloomingdale’s and come away with a very different impression of how much you’d treated yourself. Trader Joe’s has spent decades figuring out how to create the illusion for budget shoppers that they are not budget shopping, Claus Ebster, a marketer who has studied Trader Joe’s, told me. With its Tiki decor, Hawaiian shirts, and vaguely flirtatious cashiers, Trader Joe’s has a more enjoyable vibe than one might expect from a store known for selling a selection of wines for $5 or less. Its store-brand product names, too, try just a little harder than they need to: Midsummer Night’s Cream has a je ne sais quoi to which the Kirkland Signature Body Lotion can only aspire. All of this can create a halo effect around Trader Joe’s products, Gardiner told me. That positive predisposition can be especially important in beauty, when a customer needs to trust a company enough to slather its product on their face. Trader Joe’s didn’t provide me with beauty-product sales figures, but the virality of some of these items suggest that at least some people are buying in. Beyond offering similar ingredients, so much of a dupe’s value comes from how well it can replicate the texture, smell, and packaging of a luxury product. But for many younger beauty shoppers, simply being able to own a bunch of products counts as a luxury, Wolfer said. Many women now show off their Trader Joe’s hauls on social media as if they’re Sephora products worth hundreds of dollars. And ultimately, this serves TJ’s well: People seeking luxury-ish moisturizer on a tight budget will have one more reason to come to the store, and maybe pick up a frozen pizza from Italy along with a cheap bottle of wine for a nice night in. No one’s fooling themselves that this is the exact equivalent of ordering a pizza made with D.O.P. mozzarella di Bufala , opening a bottle of Greco di Tufo, and doing a home facial with $800 of La Mer products. But for many people, it’s close enough.

items.title: Maroc-Sénégal : un contact téléphonique suspect pourrait remettre en cause la validité de la sentence du TAS
items.description: Un éventuel échange téléphonique entre un arbitre du Tribunal arbitral du sport (TAS) et le président de la fédération appelante soulève des interrogations sur l'impartialité de la Formation chargée du dossier. Pour Me Mourad El Ajouti, président du Club des avocats au Maroc, si ce contact est avéré, il pourrait constituer un motif de récusation de l'arbitre et fragiliser la validité de la sentence arbitrale.** L'affaire prend une nouvelle dimension sur le terrain juridique. Après les révélations de RMC Sport faisant état d'un courrier adressé par la Fédération royale marocaine de football (FRMF) au Greffe du Tribunal arbitral du sport, concernant un contact téléphonique qui aurait eu lieu dimanche 22 novembre entre l'un des trois arbitres chargés du dossier et le président de la fédération appelante, la question de l'impartialité de la Formation arbitrale se retrouve au centre des débats. Dans une analyse juridique consacrée à cette situation, Me Mourad El Ajouti, président du Club des avocats au Maroc, estime que, si les faits sont établis, l'incident pourrait dépasser le simple cadre d'une irrégularité procédurale pour remettre en cause la régularité même de la composition du tribunal arbitral et, par conséquent, la validité de sa future sentence. L'avocat rappelle que l'impartialité et l'indépendance constituent des exigences fondamentales de l'arbitrage sportif. L'article R33 du Code du TAS impose ainsi à chaque arbitre de demeurer indépendant et impartial à l'égard des parties, tout en lui faisant obligation de révéler sans délai toute circonstance susceptible de soulever des interrogations à ce sujet. Cette exigence est également encadrée par le droit suisse, puisque le siège du TAS se trouve à Lausanne. L'article 182, alinéa 3, de la loi fédérale sur le droit international privé (LDIP) garantit notamment l'égalité des parties et le respect du principe du contradictoire. Dans ce contexte, un échange non déclaré entre un arbitre et l'une des parties, alors que le dossier se trouve en phase de délibération, pourrait constituer une atteinte à ces garanties. Selon Me El Ajouti, une telle situation romprait l'égalité des armes, dès lors que l'autre partie n'aurait pas connaissance de la teneur des échanges. Elle pourrait également contrevenir à l'obligation de révélation et faire naître un doute légitime sur l'impartialité de l'arbitre concerné. Deux voies de recours à la disposition de la FRMF Sur le plan procédural, Me El Ajouti identifie deux mécanismes juridiques susceptibles d'être mobilisés. Le premier concerne la récusation de l'arbitre. Prévue par l'article R34 du Code du TAS, cette procédure permet à toute partie de contester la participation d'un arbitre lorsque des circonstances sont de nature à faire légitimement douter de son indépendance ou de son impartialité. La demande doit être introduite dans un délai de sept jours à compter de la connaissance du motif de récusation. Elle est ensuite examinée par la Commission de récusation du Conseil international de l'arbitrage en matière de sport (CIAS). Pour le président du Club des avocats au Maroc, la démarche entreprise par la FRMF auprès du Greffe du TAS permet de signaler les faits et de préserver ses droits dans le respect du délai prévu. La seconde voie concerne un éventuel recours en annulation devant le Tribunal fédéral suisse, si la sentence venait à être rendue malgré les irrégularités dénoncées. Ce recours devrait être introduit dans un délai de trente jours et pourrait notamment s'appuyer sur deux dispositions de l'article 190, alinéa 2, de la LDIP : l'irrégularité de la composition du tribunal arbitral et la violation du principe de l'égalité des parties ou du droit d'être entendu. Me El Ajouti souligne que le Tribunal fédéral dispose, dans ce cadre, d'un pouvoir d'examen lui permettant d'apprécier si les circonstances invoquées étaient effectivement de nature à justifier la récusation de l'arbitre, indépendamment de la décision prise par les instances du TAS. Au-delà des conséquences sur la procédure, l'arbitre concerné pourrait également s'exposer à des mesures individuelles, notamment à son retrait de la liste des arbitres du TAS, en cas de manquement établi à ses obligations d'indépendance et de révélation. Le précédent Sun Yang Pour étayer son analyse, le juriste renvoie à un précédent important de la jurisprudence suisse : l'affaire du nageur chinois Sun Yang. Dans son arrêt 4A_318/2020 du 22 décembre 2020, publié aux ATF 147 III 65, le Tribunal fédéral suisse avait annulé une sentence du TAS en raison de circonstances mettant en cause l'impartialité d'un arbitre. Cette décision avait conduit à la récusation de l'arbitre concerné et au renvoi de l'affaire devant une nouvelle Formation entièrement recomposée. Pour Me Mourad El Ajouti, cette jurisprudence rappelle que les garanties d'indépendance et d'impartialité ne relèvent pas d'une simple formalité. Elles conditionnent la légitimité même de la justice arbitrale. Si le contact téléphonique signalé par la FRMF venait à être confirmé et à répondre aux critères retenus par le droit suisse, ses conséquences pourraient ainsi dépasser largement le cadre d'un incident de procédure. The post Maroc-Sénégal : un contact téléphonique suspect pourrait remettre en cause la validité de la sentence du TAS appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: GABS 2026: Mahama urges fellow African leaders to strengthen policy consistency, accountability to attract investment
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has urged his fellow African leaders to strengthen policy consistency, institutional reforms and accountability to make the continent more attractive to international investors. He said Africa must demonstrate its readiness to attract investment through deliberate policies, strong institutions and actions that create an enabling environment for businesses to thrive. According to him, “To my fellow African leaders here, we must demonstrate through our policies, our institutions, and actions that Africa is ready to attract investments and translate them into shared prosperity,” he said at the Presidential Opening Addresses of the 6th German-African Business Summit (GABS 2026) in Accra on Tuesday, November 24. President Mahama said Africa needed to address structural challenges that undermine its competitiveness and ability to attract sustainable investments. He identified policy consistency, institutional reforms, regional integration, democracy, accountability and infrastructure development as critical foundations for building competitive African economies. President Mahama said stronger economic cooperation between Germany and Africa could deliver significant benefits to both regions, given their complementary economic strengths. He noted that while Germany stood to benefit from opportunities to diversify supply chains, develop new markets and establish sustainable industrial partnerships, African countries could leverage German investment, innovation and technical expertise to accelerate industrialisation. According to him, such partnerships could improve productivity and efficiency, strengthen skills development and enhance the competitiveness of African economies. “Our task is to bring these complementary strengths of Africa and Germany together, to deliver mutual lasting benefits through partnerships between our entrepreneurs, the establishment of manufacturing enterprises, the development of our infrastructure, and the processing of our agricultural and mineral resources,” he said. He added that Africa must move beyond exporting raw materials and focus on developing industries capable of competing in the global marketplace. The President expressed optimism about the future of German-African economic relations, saying the next phase of cooperation should prioritise economies that reward enterprise, welcome innovation and provide stable and competitive environments for responsible investment. He urged participants at the summit to use the platform to develop practical partnerships and identify opportunities that would translate into sustainable economic growth. The 6th German-African Business Summit, which runs from November 23 to 25, 2026, is bringing together government officials, business executives, investors and industry experts from Germany and across Africa. The summit is focusing on investment opportunities and economic cooperation in sectors including energy transition, green hydrogen, digitalisation, artificial intelligence, automotive, mining, trade finance and industrial development.

items.title: Israeli strikes in Gaza kill 7, including senior security official
items.description: Israeli airstrikes in Gaza on Tuesday killed seven people, including Hamas’s director of internal security, Palestinian officials in the territory told AFP, despite a ceasefire in place since last year. Israel’s military said it had struck a senior Hamas official. Gaza’s interior ministry said an airstrike in Gaza City killed Brigadier General Naeem Abu Nahal, director-general of the Internal Security Service. Mahmoud Bassal, spokesman for Gaza’s civil defence agency, told AFP that several other people were in critical condition following the same strike in Gaza City’s Rimal neighbourhood. The strike comes as talks are underway in Israel to form a new government after October legislative elections produced no clear winner. Centrist Gadi Eisenkot wants to form a coalition to end caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s long tenure. But Netanyahu, who has staked his reputation on ensuring security for Israel after the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023, remains in charge of military operations while negotiations continue. Police station strike Bassal said earlier on Tuesday that three people, including a 17-year-old, had been killed in a separate Israeli airstrike near Gaza City. Three more were also killed in a third airstrike on a police station in the Al-Mawasi area in southern Gaza, he added. Gaza’s police force said two policemen aged 23 and 33 were among the dead. It condemned the strike as “part of an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus”. Israel’s military said it “struck terrorists in the area” of the police station, but did not confirm the strike that killed the 17-year-old. Israel and Hamas regularly accuse each other of violating the ceasefire that came into effect in October 2025, after two years of war triggered by the October 2023 attack. More than 1,650 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the truce, according to an AFP tally based on data from the Gaza health ministry. In the same period, the Israeli military says seven of its soldiers have been killed, as well as one civilian contractor. Most of Gaza’s population of 2.1 million live displaced in tents or makeshift shelters in the territory, where Israel’s military says it controls more than 60 per cent of the land.

items.title: Beyond compliance: Turning cocoa traceability into a global competitive advantage for Ghana
items.description: For decades, Ghana’s cocoa has enjoyed international recognition for its quality, consistency and reliability. These attributes have sustained our commercial relationships and earned Ghanaian cocoa a respected place in the world’s chocolate and confectionery industries. However, the global cocoa market is changing. Increasingly, buyers are concerned not only about the quality of cocoa they purchase but also about its origin, the circumstances under which it was produced and the integrity of the supply chain through which it reaches them. This represents a significant transformation in international commodity trading. And for Ghana, it presents an opportunity that extends far beyond regulatory compliance. We are entering an era in which the ability to demonstrate the origin of a commodity is becoming almost as important as the commodity itself. Our responsibility is to ensure that Ghana is strategically positioned to benefit from it and not merely respond to it. Regulatory Obligation to Commercial Opportunity The European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) has accelerated the global conversation about traceability, environmental responsibility and transparency in agricultural supply chains. With the regulation scheduled to apply to medium and large operators from 30 December 2026, cocoa-producing countries are being challenged to demonstrate that the cocoa entering the European market satisfies applicable deforestation and legality requirements. Naturally, much of the conversation has concentrated on the cost of compliance, the technological requirements and the potential consequences for countries that fail to meet the new standards. These concerns are legitimate. However, viewing traceability exclusively through the lens of regulation would mean overlooking its wider commercial value. A credible traceability system offers buyers something that increasingly matters in international trade: the confidence backed by verifiable information. For manufacturers managing complex supply chains, information about the origin and movement of cocoa is an important instrument for managing risk, satisfying regulatory requirements and protecting corporate reputation. Ghana already possesses important institutional advantages in this regard. Our regulated cocoa marketing system, our established quality control procedures and coordinated export arrangements provide a foundation upon which more sophisticated traceability capabilities will be developed. The Ghana Cocoa Traceability System (GCTS), whose nationwide deployment was announced by COCOBOD in September 2026, is an important step in strengthening this foundation. At Cocoa Marketing Company (Ghana) Limited, our involvement in the implementation of traceability is particularly important because of our position between Ghana’s cocoa supply chain and the international marketplace. Our Take-Over Centres represent critical points in the movement of cocoa from producing communities towards export destinations. The integrity of traceability information is therefore being preserved as cocoa moves through aggregation, inspection, warehousing and shipment. We have put in place an operational framework in which physical cocoa movements and their corresponding digital records reinforce one another. When the documentation supporting a consignment is accurate, accessible and verifiable, we strengthen the confidence of buyers and reduce avoidable uncertainty in commercial transactions. This is the practical connection between traceability and competitiveness. Turning Information into Market Value There is another dimension to this transformation that deserves attention. Traceability data can become an important commercial resource when it is responsibly managed and effectively integrated into market intelligence. Over time, credible supply-chain information can help support product differentiation, improve inventory visibility, strengthen buyer engagement and inform more responsive trading decisions. It can also provide a stronger foundation for discussions about verified origin, sustainability performance and responsible sourcing arrangements. Our focus will therefore remain on making Ghana’s traceability credentials commercially meaningful. We are strengthening the connection between operational information and the needs of our international customers, working within the wider COCOBOD framework and our institutional responsibilities. Equally important is the protection of farmers whose production activities generate much of the underlying information. Data governance, accessibility and fair participation will remain central to the implementation process. A modern traceability system cannot fulfil its purpose if the people at the beginning of the value chain are disadvantaged by it. Ghana’s Opportunity to Lead The future of international cocoa trade will increasingly reward producing countries that can combine quality, dependable supply and credible information. At CMC, we recognise that preserving Ghana’s international cocoa reputation now requires excellence in both physical commodity management and the information systems that support it. We will continue to play our part in strengthening operational readiness, supporting the implementation of national traceability initiatives and maintaining the confidence of our international trading partners.

items.title: WFP Kenya Country Brief, November 2026
items.description: Countries: Kenya, Ethiopia, Somalia Source: World Food Programme Please refer to the attached file. SITUATION OVERVIEW • October was marked by overlapping humanitarian pressures, with worsening drought conditions in several arid and semi-arid counties, continued concerns over acute malnutrition, and a new influx of people fleeing conflict in Ethiopia into Moyale. While above-average rainfall forecast for the October– December short-rains season offer prospects for improved water availability, pasture and crop production, it also heightens the risk of flooding and landslides, particularly in flood-prone areas of Garissa and Tana River counties, including Dadaab refugee camp. Meanwhile, approximately 30,000 new arrivals from Ethiopia were profiled in Moyale, with urgent needs for food, water, healthcare, shelter and protection. These overlapping pressures underscored the need for simultaneous drought preparedness, anticipatory action against flooding, and emergency assistance for newly displaced populations. OPERATIONAL UPDATES Refugee assistance • In September, WFP provided food and cash assistance to 623,000 refugees and asylum seekers in Dadaab, Kakuma and Kalobeyei, covering their September and October entitlements. However, funding shortages have forced WFP to reduce food rations for the most vulnerable households and those with limited capacity to meet basic needs from 80 and 60 percent of the minimum food basket, to 60 and 40 percent, respectively. Rations for partially selfreliant households remain at 20 percent.

items.title: Justice sportive mondiale : Kéba Mbaye, le Sénégalais qui a donné naissance au TAS
items.description: À l'heure où le Sénégal se retrouve devant le Tribunal arbitral du sport (TAS) dans son bras de fer avec le Maroc, un pan méconnu de l'histoire de cette juridiction mérite d'être rappelé. Cette institution, devenue incontournable dans le règlement des litiges sportifs internationaux, porte une empreinte sénégalaise considérable. Son histoire est intimement liée à un magistrat d'exception : Kéba Mbaye. L'idée initiale revient à Juan Antonio Samaranch, président du Comité international olympique (CIO) à partir de 1980. Mais entre concevoir une idée et lui donner une existence juridique et institutionnelle, il y a un travail considérable. C'est précisément dans cette étape décisive que le Sénégalais Kéba Mbaye a joué un rôle déterminant. En 1982, le CIO constitue un groupe de travail chargé de mettre en place cette nouvelle juridiction. À sa tête, Kéba Mbaye, alors magistrat à la Cour internationale de justice et membre du mouvement olympique. Sa mission consiste à traduire le projet de Samaranch en une institution opérationnelle, dotée de règles et de statuts. Sous sa conduite, les fondements juridiques du futur tribunal sont élaborés. Les premiers statuts sont ratifiés en 1983. Le 30 juin 1984, le TAS devient officiellement opérationnel. Kéba Mbaye en devient le premier président. Son rôle ne s'arrête pas à cette naissance institutionnelle. Il dirige le tribunal pendant plus de vingt ans, jusqu'à son décès en janvier 2007, accompagnant son développement et son affirmation progressive dans le paysage sportif international. En 1984, il publie également dans l'Annuaire français de droit international un article consacré à cette nouvelle institution d'arbitrage. Une contribution qui témoigne de son implication intellectuelle dans la conception de cette juridiction. Le parcours de Kéba Mbaye éclaire la confiance placée en lui. Ancien premier président de la Cour suprême du Sénégal et vice-président de la Cour internationale de justice à La Haye de 1981 à 1990, il était l'un des juristes africains les plus respectés de son époque. Son expertise a été déterminante pour donner au TAS ses fondements et sa crédibilité juridique. L'institution a certes évolué depuis sa création. En 1994, une réforme conduit à la mise en place du Conseil international de l'arbitrage en matière de sport (CIAS), chargé notamment de garantir l'indépendance du TAS vis-à-vis du CIO. Mais cette évolution n'efface en rien l'héritage de son premier architecte. Quarante-deux ans après ses débuts, le TAS est devenu une référence mondiale, appelé à trancher les contentieux les plus sensibles du sport, du dopage aux sanctions disciplinaires, en passant par les litiges contractuels et les conflits entre fédérations. Dans le contexte du différend Sénégal-Maroc, cette histoire prend une résonance particulière. Le Sénégal défend aujourd'hui ses intérêts devant une juridiction dont l'un des principaux bâtisseurs fut un de ses illustres fils. Ce rappel historique ne constitue évidemment ni un argument juridique ni une garantie sur l'issue du dossier. Il souligne cependant la contribution remarquable d'un Sénégalais à la construction d'une institution qui occupe désormais une place centrale dans la gouvernance du sport mondial. Le TAS n'est pas une création exclusivement sénégalaise. Mais dans sa conception juridique, sa mise en place et ses premières années de fonctionnement, l’empreinte de Kéba Mbaye est si profonde qu'elle mérite d'être pleinement reconnue. Le Sénégal peut légitimement s'enorgueillir d'avoir contribué, à travers l'un de ses plus illustres magistrats, à bâtir l'une des institutions majeures de la justice sportive internationale. Cheikh Gora DIOP

items.title: CRADAT : Ramatoulaye Camara lance les travaux des experts en prélude à la 45e session ordinaire du Conseil d’administration
items.description: La Guinée renoue avec les sessions ordinaires du Centre régional africain de l’administration du travail (CRADAT), après près de trois décennies d’absence. La ministre guinéenne de l’Emploi, du Travail et de la Protection sociale, Ramatoulaye Camara, a donné, ce mardi 24 novembre 2026, le coup d’envoi des travaux des experts, en prélude à la 45e session ordinaire du Conseil d’administration de l’institution. La cérémonie s’est déroulée à Conakry, en présence de son homologue sénégalais de la Fonction et du Travail, ainsi que du directeur général du CRADAT, Arsène Armand Hien. Cette rencontre technique constitue une étape importante dans la préparation de la session ministérielle prévue jeudi prochain. Elle permettra aux experts d’examiner les conclusions de la précédente session extraordinaire, de vérifier la conformité des décisions et recommandations adoptées et de préparer un rapport destiné aux ministres. Dans son allocution d’ouverture, la ministre Ramatoulaye Camara a souhaité la bienvenue aux délégations présentes en Guinée, qu’elle a présentée comme une terre d’hospitalité, de richesse et d’innovation, ouverte au monde. « Au nom de Son Excellence Monsieur le Président de la République, Monsieur Mamadi Doumbouya, et au nom du Chef du gouvernement, Monsieur Amadou Oury Bah, je voudrais vous exprimer toute notre satisfaction de vous accueillir à Conakry », a-t-elle déclaré. La ministre a également souligné le caractère particulier de cette rencontre, rappelant que la Guinée n’avait plus accueilli cette importante activité depuis 1997. Elle a invité les participants à mettre leur expertise au service de l’institution, en misant sur la qualité des échanges et la pertinence des recommandations qui seront soumises aux ministres. « Je compte, nous comptons donc sur l'expertise de tous, sur la qualité des échanges et la pertinence de vos recommandations pour contribuer au rayonnement de notre institution commune », a-t-elle insisté. Au-delà des travaux, la ministre a exprimé le souhait de voir les délégations découvrir les réalités et les ambitions de la Guinée, notamment à travers son programme de développement socio-économique et durable, Simandou 2040. Prenant la parole à son tour, le directeur général du CRADAT, Arsène Armand Hien, s’est réjoui du retour de l’institution à Conakry après 29 ans d’absence. Il a qualifié cette rencontre d’historique, soulignant le rôle joué par la Guinée dans la relance des sessions ordinaires du Conseil d’administration. « Le CRADAT est heureux que ça soit la Guinée qui a remis sur les rails la session ordinaire. C'est bon de le préciser et de le relever », a-t-il affirmé. Selon lui, les experts auront pour mission de reprendre le rapport de la session extraordinaire afin de s’assurer que les décisions et recommandations retenues sont conformes aux conclusions précédemment arrêtées. Le rapport issu de ces travaux sera ensuite transmis à la session ministérielle, qui se tiendra jeudi. Le directeur général a salué l’engagement de la Guinée, dont l’accueil marque une nouvelle étape dans le fonctionnement de cette institution régionale. Le ministre sénégalais de la Fonction et du Travail a, pour sa part, exprimé sa satisfaction de prendre part à cette rencontre à Conakry. Il a salué l’accueil réservé à sa délégation et remercié son homologue guinéenne pour les dispositions prises en vue de leur séjour. Évoquant les relations professionnelles déjà nouées entre les deux pays, il a rappelé les échanges antérieurs entre le Conseil du dialogue social du Sénégal et le Conseil national du dialogue social (CNDS) de Guinée. Le ministre sénégalais a également insisté sur l’importance du CRADAT dans l’évolution des administrations du travail en Afrique. « Je crois qu'aujourd'hui un centre d'une importance capitale que constitue donc le CRADAT a besoin quand même d'aller vers la modernisation de l'administration du travail », a-t-il souligné. Tout en saluant le travail accompli par le directeur général et son équipe, il a exprimé sa confiance dans la capacité des experts à produire un rapport de qualité, susceptible de faciliter les travaux de la session ministérielle. La tenue de cette 45e session ordinaire à Conakry intervient ainsi dans un contexte marqué par la volonté des États membres de renforcer la coopération régionale et de promouvoir une administration du travail plus moderne, efficace et adaptée aux défis du continent. Youssouf Keita L’article CRADAT : Ramatoulaye Camara lance les travaux des experts en prélude à la 45e session ordinaire du Conseil d’administration est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Fortune Spread celebrates World Children’s Day with over 700 pupils at La Bawaleshie Primary School
items.description: Wilmar Africa’s Fortune Spread brings smiles, nourishment and learning to pupils through a memorable World Children’s Day celebration. In a heartwarming celebration of childhood, learning and healthy eating, Wilmar Africa Limited, through its Fortune Spread brand, joined more than 700 pupils of La Bawaleshie Primary School to commemorate World Children’s Day. The celebration brought together pupils, teachers and the Fortune Spread team for an engaging day filled with fun activities, interaction, learning and meaningful moments aimed at celebrating children and reinforcing the importance of their health, nutrition and educational development. As part of the initiative, every participating pupil received a tasting experience featuring bread served with Fortune Spread, giving the children an opportunity to enjoy its delicious, creamy taste while experiencing the brand’s promise of making everyday bread moments more enjoyable. The pupils also received exercise books and pencils to support their learning and encourage their continued commitment to education. Beyond the fun and excitement, the engagement provided an opportunity for Fortune Spread to reinforce an important message: good nutrition and education are essential building blocks for every child’s growth and development. Seven Essential Vitamins. One Delicious Spread. A key highlight of the engagement was the opportunity to educate pupils and the wider school community about the nutritional value of Fortune Spread. Fortune Spread is enriched with seven essential vitamins: Vitamins A, D, E, B6, B12, Folic Acid and Niacin, which play important roles in supporting normal body functions, growth and development. Together, these seven essential vitamins make Fortune Spread a thoughtful addition to everyday family meals, offering more than just a delicious taste. While no single food provides everything a growing child needs, incorporating nutritious food choices into a balanced and varied diet is an important step towards supporting children’s overall wellbeing. Making Every Bread Moment Delicious and Meaningful Fortune Spread’s participation in World Children’s Day reflects the brand’s positioning as a delicious, creamy and vitamin-enriched spread for bread, bringing together taste and nutritional value in a product families can enjoy as part of their everyday meals. Whether at breakfast, during school breaks or as a convenient snack at home, Fortune Spread seeks to make ordinary bread moments more enjoyable while contributing to the variety of foods families include in their daily diets. The brand believes that children deserve access to enjoyable food experiences while parents and caregivers remain mindful of the nutritional choices they make for their families. By taking this message directly to La Bawaleshie Primary School, Fortune Spread demonstrated its commitment to connecting with consumers beyond the supermarket shelf and becoming part of the everyday experiences that matter to Ghanaian families. Investing in Children, Investing in the Future The distribution of exercise books and pencils further underscored the brand’s recognition that children’s development extends beyond nutrition. Education remains one of the most important investments society can make in shaping confident, knowledgeable and responsible future generations. For Wilmar Africa, the engagement was an opportunity to celebrate children, create positive brand experiences and contribute meaningfully to the communities in which it operates. As the world celebrates children and recognises their rights to education, good health, protection and opportunities to thrive, Fortune Spread remains committed to creating delightful food experiences that bring families together. This World Children’s Day, Fortune Spread celebrates every child, every dream and every opportunity to grow. Because every child deserves a delicious start and a brighter future. Fortune Spread – Delicious Goodness in Every Slice!

items.title: 'Watching me with eyes of fire': Pope Francis revealed in personal diary having seen devil
items.description: The late Pope Francis recounted seeing the devil three times and, on one occasion, the “gate of hell”, in excerpts from his personal diary published on Tuesday in a new book. The Private Diary of Pope Francis , by Argentine Cardinal Victor Manuel Fernandez, includes passages taken from a journal the former Jorge Bergoglio kept between 1992 and 2024, a document that reveals his worries, regrets and self-critiques — as well as his enormous humanity and faith. Fernandez, head of the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, said he was asked by Francis to help make known to the world the musings inside the black plastic journal. Upon Francis’s death last year, Fernandez expressed concern to his successor, Leo XIV, that the book “might end up abandoned in a warehouse somewhere”. He was allowed to publish passages, noting that “the spiritual concerns present in his heart are very explicit and can be helpful to us”. In one of the most intriguing revelations, Francis writes that while archbishop of Buenos Aires, he saw the devil three different times including “from the car when I was returning to the house, and in the choir loft during Mass” and once in Rome following a visit to Chile. “I discovered that the devil had been brazenly lurking around cunningly,” wrote Francis in his journal on January 24, 2021, according to a copy of the English language version of the book published by Penguin Random House and viewed by AFP . Francis wrote that he recalled three episodes “when I don’t doubt he was physically present”. “More or less fifteen years ago. I saw him from the car window. I can’t forget his menacing and, at the same time, seductive eyes,” he wrote. During the second episode inside a Carmelite chapel, Francis wrote: “He was watching me with eyes of fire”. “I can’t forget that gaze, stronger than the previous. They were like flames of fire.” The third episode occurred during a meeting in Rome, following a visit to Chile. “I saw him and heard his voice, triumphant, possessing everything… I can’t forget the powerful raspiness of his voice,” he wrote, adding that “the Lord granted me an opportunity to leave that meeting, and he thus freed me”. Francis also revealed, on June 7, 2018, that on the night before, while getting ready to go to sleep, he “saw the entrance to hell”. “Pagan seduction in full force. I peeked in to look a little, and it terrified me,” he said, adding that he “grabbed the Rosary as a weapon”. “It’s dangerous to approach the gate of hell because flames can leap out and burn,” he wrote. Self critiques Throughout the diary, Francis does not hesitate to criticise himself, for his occasional “feelings of disdain, envy, pride” or for having ignored a drunk man in the street who addressed him “because I wanted to have a serene walk”. “The proud, self-sufficient, cynical, self-deceptive Jorge” is how the former pope described himself on December 30, 2022. On January 15, 2017, he confessed that for a few days he had been experiencing “a very bad spirit of anger and discontent”. While charismatic, Pope Francis also had a strong personality and was sometimes criticised within the Curia, the Catholic Church’s governing body, for being authoritarian. Mercy is a recurrent theme in the journal. “I felt, looking back, all the evil I’ve done in life. I’m in such abundant need of the Lord’s mercy!” he wrote on January 5, 1997. End of life Pope Francis appeared to worry that his days on Earth would be short-lived, fretting over his ageing and the need to “bear it”. In 1996, at age 60 — nearly three decades before his death — he wrote: “I want to do good during the little time I have left, desiring to be good. “How much time I’ve used badly! How much badly done!” In 2001, he wrote that “these 65 years make me think about the end. I’m already counting down”. The worries continued even after becoming pope in 2013, with Francis writing on April 9, 2016 that “the attacks of the devil under different aspects have increased… Could it be a sign that my time is up and he doesn’t want to lose?” The journal contains 86 pages written before his election as pope in 2013, and another 55 written afterwards. One of the briefest — and most moving — passages in Francis’s diary comes on July 21, 2013: “On March 13, they elected me pope.” Francis died on April 21, 2025.

items.title: Yendi MP wants schools held responsible for early BECE candidates
items.description: The Member of Parliament for Yendi, Alhassan Abdul-Fatawu, has called on the government to hold schools and educational authorities accountable for presenting pupils to sit the Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE) before their designated examination year, rather than penalising the students. He argued that institutions responsible for preparing and presenting candidates should bear the consequences of early examination attempts, insisting that pupils should not be made to suffer for decisions influenced by their schools. Mr Abdul-Fatawu made the call during an interview on JoyNews’ AM Show on Tuesday, November 24, amid the government’s decision to impose a two-year examination ban on pupils who attempt to write the BECE ahead of their designated year. According to the MP, the policy should target the institutions facilitating the practice, which he believes are in a better position to prevent pupils from sitting the examination prematurely. “We can blacklist institutions that present such candidates. Rather than the student,” he said. He maintained that parents who seek to have their children sit the examination early are often responding to opportunities created by schools and other institutions, making it necessary for authorities to address the problem at its source. Mr Abdul-Fatawu argued that penalising pupils would not adequately address the underlying issue if schools continued to facilitate early examination attempts. He therefore called for stronger measures to close what he described as loopholes in the system that allow institutions to present candidates before they are due to write the examination. The Yendi MP further proposed that heads of schools and officials of the Ghana Education Service (GES) should be held responsible where institutions under their supervision present pupils for the BECE prematurely. He said accountability should extend beyond private schools to public institutions, stressing that school leadership and education administrators must have a direct responsibility for ensuring compliance with examination regulations. “Let the owner or the institution, in fact, if it is not a private school and it’s a government school, the head of the school, and if possible the GES director and all those people should have their assessment tied to this thing,” he stated. He suggested that the performance assessments of relevant school heads and GES directors should be linked to compliance with the rules governing the presentation of candidates for the national examination. His proposal, he indicated, would ensure that those responsible for administering schools and supervising the education system are directly accountable for preventing premature examination attempts. Government introduces two-year BECE examination ban Mr Abdul-Fatawu’s comments come after the Minister for Education, Haruna Iddrisu, directed the Ghana Education Service to impose a two-year examination ban on pupils who attempt to sit the BECE before their designated examination year. The directive is intended to discourage early examination attempts and ensure that pupils follow the approved educational progression before taking the national assessment. However, he believes holding schools and their officials accountable would help address the problem at its source and discourage institutions from presenting candidates for the examination ahead of schedule.

items.title: Bond market: Turnover declines by 16% to GH¢5.72bn
items.description: The secondary bond market turnover moderated by 16.65% week-on-week to GH¢5.72 billion. Trading activity was concentrated in the 2027-2030 maturity segment, which accounted for 65.35% of total turnover at a weighted-average yield of 12.41%. The 2031-2034 segment followed with a 32.86% share at a weighted-average yield of 14.75%. Post-2035 maturities accounted for just 1.78% of turnover at a weighted-average yield of 14.59%. Separately, the Government of Ghana opened a voluntary buyback of up to GH¢28.58 billion in February 2027 Domestic Debt Exchange Programme (DDEP) bonds on 23 November 2026, using a multiple-clearing yield mechanism. The offer closes at 3:00 p.m. on 25 November, with settlement scheduled for 26 November 2026. Databank Research said, “ We expect investor participation in the buyback to reflect investors’ liquidity needs, reinvestment considerations, and month-end cash requirements. Given the bond’s last traded YTM [Yield-To-Maturity] of 11.24% and relatively lower short-term yields, we believe buy-and-hold investors may be reluctant to accept significant price discounts, while month-end liquidity pressures could encourage more competitive offers from cash-constrained investors”. Against this backdrop, it anticipates subdued secondary market activity in the near term as investors await the auction results for clearer pricing signals before repositioning their portfolios.
